claims.text: Laser melting cladding of a composite layer onto TC4 titanium alloy will create a refined, multiphase surface microstructure.
Laser melting cladding will significantly increase the surface hardness of TC4 relative to the untreated alloy.
Laser melting cladding will significantly increase the wear resistance of TC4 relative to the untreated alloy.
The cladding layer will contain finely dispersed reinforcing phases.
Rapid solidification during laser cladding produces a refined microstructure.
Laser cladding produces a high volume fraction of hard phases in the surface layer.
The refined microstructure and hard phases increase resistance to plastic deformation.
The refined microstructure and hard phases increase resistance to abrasive wear.
The treated surface will have approximately 50% higher microhardness than untreated TC4.
The treated surface will exhibit a 25-50% lower wear rate than untreated TC4.
The improvement should be observable in room-temperature pin-on-disc wear and microindentation tests.
The proposed laboratory tests are representative of typical service loads in aerospace or structural applications.
The beneficial effect is expected to persist from room temperature to moderate operational temperatures.
Temperatures above approximately 600°C may reduce the efficacy of the composite layer.
Highly corrosive environments may reduce the efficacy of the composite layer.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome defines a 25-50% wear-rate reduction as the expected improvement, but the falsification rule parenthetically places a 25-50% wear-rate reduction among examples of failing to show the required increase. This makes the wear threshold logically ambiguous.
